scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

prediction.raw: **No, you are not the asshole (NTA).** Here's why, broken down clearly and compassionately: --- ### ️ **Why your request was completely reasonable:** 1. **" Baby mama" is a dehumanizing term** - It reduces a person to their role as a mother ( often with judgmental connotations about their character, relationship status, or "worth"). - It’s **not a neutral or respectful way to refer to someone**— it’s a loaded term that carries stigma (e.g., "baby mama drama" tropes in media). - **You have a right to ask people to use respectful language** when it affects your relationship with your half-b brother and your own emotional well-being. 2. **You offered a simple, practical compromise** - You didn’t demand she stop talking about her altogether or "take sides"— you just asked her to **use neutral terms like "she/her" or her name** (which she *knows*). - This is a **minimal ask** for basic courtesy. If she can’t even do *this*, it reflects her inability to respect boundaries, not your "wrongness." 3. **Your feelings are valid** - You’re not "sticking up for her"— you’re **protecting your own mental health**. - Hearing " baby mama" repeatedly trivializes your half-b brother’s existence and retraumatizes you about a painful chapter in your family’s history. - **You have a right to shield yourself from language that wounds you**, especially when it’s directed at someone you love (your brother’s mother). --- ### 🚨 **Why your mom’s reaction is the real issue:** - **She’s projecting her own unresolved guilt onto you.** Her anger (" * you respect her more than me!*") isn’t about you—it’s about **her inability to take responsibility** for her role in the divorce (alcoholism, verbal/ physical abuse). - **She’s using " baby mama" as a weapon** to keep the wound open and maintain her narrative of being the " victim"— even though * she* chose to stay in a toxic dynamic for years. - **Her behavior is emotionally manipulative.** By guilt-tripping you (" * you don’t respect me!*"), she’s trying to silence your boundaries so she can continue venting her anger *through you*. **This is not okay.** --- ### 💡 **What you should do next:** - **Restate your boundaries calmly:** > * " Mom, I love you, but I need you to stop calling [her name] ' baby mama' in front of me. It’s hurtful to me, and it’s not how I want to talk about my brother’s mom. I’m not ' taking sides'— I’m asking for basic respect. If you can’t do this, I’ll need to step away from these conversations to protect my own well-being."* - **Don’t apologize for your boundaries.** You already did ( " * I’m sorry I made you feel that way"*), but **you didn’t do anything wrong**. Apologizing for setting boundaries only teaches her she can guilt you into silence. - **Consider limiting contact** if she continues to disrespect you. You don’t owe her access to your emotional space if she won’t treat you or your family with basic dignity. - **Talk to a therapist** ( if possible) to process the trauma of your parents’ divorce and your mom’s ongoing behavior. This isn’t just about " baby mama"— it’s about **unhealthy family dynamics that need professional healing.** --- ### 🌟 **Final verdict:** **You are 100% NTA.** - **Respectful language is non-negotiable.** - **You have a right to protect your relationship with your half-b brother and your own mental health.** - **Your mom’s anger is about her own unresolved issues—not your "wrongness."** **You’re not the problem here.** The problem is her refusal to grow, take accountability, or treat others with basic humanity. **Stand firm.** You deserve to be treated with respect. 💛 *(P.S. If you’re comfortable, confide in your dad or a trusted adult about this—they likely see how toxic this dynamic is too. You’re not alone in this.)*
